The Week the Guardrails Were Tested

Law firms, judges, students, and federal workers all came under direct executive pressure this week — while a leaked war-plan chat exposed how casually power was being handled behind closed doors

```markdown This was a week in which nearly every institutional check on presidential power was tested at once, and in which the pressure ran in both directions — coercion from the White House met, unevenly but persistently, by lawsuits, injunctions, and public resistance. Law firms were punished for representing the president's opponents. A federal judge was defied over deportation flights and then threatened with impeachment. Students were detained for political speech. A voting-rules order threatened to complicate registration for millions. And in the middle of it all, a magazine editor found himself accidentally added to a group chat where the nation's most senior security officials were discussing live strike plans on a commercial messaging app.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set the tone. Trump issued executive orders against the law firms Perkins Coie and Covington & Burling, extending a campaign that had already hit Paul Weiss, and the White House revoked security clearances for sixteen former officials. The stated justification was that these firms had represented his opponents or employed lawyers tied to investigations against him; the practical effect was to make representing the administration's adversaries carry a cost. At the same time, Trump publicly denied signing his own deportation proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act, even though his signature appeared in the Federal Register — a small but telling episode in a week full of questions about who was actually directing consequential policy. Judge James Boasberg, meanwhile, opened an inquiry into whether the administration had defied his order halting deportation flights; 137 Venezuelan migrants had been deported anyway, and officials, including deportation czar Tom Homan, said openly that they did not care what the judge thought. Trump compared Tesla vandalism to the January 6 attack and called for twenty-year sentences, months after pardoning convicted January 6 rioters — a jarring contrast in how political violence was being treated depending on its target. He also pressured Maine Governor Janet Mills over her refusal to comply with a transgender sports ban, threatening the state's federal funding. Beneath these clashes, a "TeslaTakedown" protest movement was gathering strength, and a Harris Poll found one in five Americans planning permanent boycotts of companies aligned with the administration's agenda.

**Monday**

By Monday, the week's most consequential single revelation had surfaced: The Atlantic's Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been mistakenly added to a Signal chat in which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Vice President JD Vance, and other senior officials discussed detailed operational plans for strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen — on an unsecured commercial app, with messages set to auto-delete. It was, on its face, a serious operational security failure, and it would occupy the week's remaining days. The same day, Trump signed an order directing the Education Secretary to begin dismantling the Department of Education, while Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced plans to eliminate FEMA, the government's primary disaster-response agency — both attempts to use executive action to accomplish what would normally require Congress. Attorney General Pam Bondi warned Democratic Representative Jasmine Crockett to "tread very carefully" after she supported a Tesla protest rally, and separately labeled pro-Palestinian student protesters "domestic terrorists." A 21-year-old Columbia green card holder, Yunseo Chung, sued the administration after ICE tried to arrest and deport her over her participation in campus protests, alleging retaliation for protected speech. Trump named his former personal attorney, Alina Habba, who had no prosecutorial experience, as interim U.S. Attorney for New Jersey; she said she intended to help "turn New Jersey red." And the Department of Government Efficiency fired 11,000 IRS employees, part of a broader cut expected to reach 20,000 workers and reduce federal tax revenue by roughly $500 billion this year.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday deepened several of these threads at once. Trump signed a sweeping executive order overhauling federal election rules, requiring documentary proof of citizenship for voter registration and threatening funding cuts to noncompliant states — despite noncitizen voting being exceedingly rare and roughly 21 million eligible voters lacking ready proof of citizenship on hand. The law firm campaign expanded again, with a new order suspending security clearances and terminating federal contracts for Jenner & Block, which employed former special counsel deputy Andrew Weissmann. The pattern of targeting political speech through immigration enforcement widened as well: Tufts doctoral student Rumeysa Ozturk was detained and transferred to Louisiana in apparent violation of a court notice requirement after co-authoring a pro-Palestinian op-ed, and University of Alabama student Alireza Doroudi was detained without stated justification. The State Department expanded visa screening based on applicants' social media activity. But the day also brought a check: a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking ICE from detaining or transferring Yunseo Chung, finding the government had not shown sufficient basis for its claims. And the Signal chat fallout intensified as the watchdog group American Oversight sued Hegseth and other officials for violating federal record-keeping law, while Hegseth, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, and Trump himself all publicly denied that classified information had been shared — denials that would not survive contact with the primary source.

**Wednesday**

By Wednesday, that source arrived: The Atlantic published the actual screenshots, contradicting the officials' denials outright. Also that day, Columbia University, having lost $400 million in federal funding, agreed to overhaul its protest policies and hire an internal security force empowered to remove people from campus — a concession that alarmed faculty concerned about academic freedom. A federal appeals court, in a split decision, upheld Judge Boasberg's block on further deportations under the Alien Enemies Act, even though the administration had already deported hundreds of people without complying with his earlier order to turn planes around. House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters that Congress had the authority to "eliminate an entire district court," as House Republicans pursued impeachment resolutions against judges who had ruled against the administration — a direct escalation from criticizing rulings to floating the elimination of courts themselves. And in a smaller but telling moment, Fox News stopped putting national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin on air after she accurately reported that the Signal chat contained sensitive operational details, not vague generalities.

**Thursday**

Thursday brought the week's largest single blow to organized labor: an executive order excluded dozens of federal agencies from labor-management relations coverage, citing national security grounds, and stripped collective bargaining protections from more than a million federal workers. The administration simultaneously sued unions in Texas to affirm its authority to void existing bargaining agreements outright. The same day, a separate order titled "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History" directed Vice President Vance to remove content on race and gender from Smithsonian museums and restore pre-2020 Confederate monuments, conditioning future funding on ideological compliance. The law firm campaign reached a fifth target, WilmerHale, whose order cited its employment of former special counsel Robert Mueller and its pro bono immigration and voting rights work. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced roughly 10,000 additional layoffs at HHS, bringing total losses across the FDA, CDC, and NIH to around 20,000 workers. Judge Boasberg, acting on the watchdog lawsuit, ordered officials to preserve all Signal communications from the relevant days and file a status report on compliance. And new messages surfaced suggesting Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller had invoked presidential authority to greenlight the Yemen strike, while Vance indicated uncertainty about whether Trump himself was fully aware of the decision — raising a pointed question about who, precisely, held the authority being exercised.

**Friday**

Friday showed the law firm campaign splitting into two distinct paths. Jenner & Block and WilmerHale filed federal lawsuits challenging the orders against them as unconstitutional retaliation, joining a resistance track. Skadden Arps, by contrast, reached a preemptive $100 million settlement, following Paul Weiss's earlier capitulation. And Perkins Coie won an actual court block on its order — the first successful legal challenge to the entire campaign, proof that the strategy was not unstoppable. Elsewhere, the University of Michigan closed its diversity office, which had measurably increased enrollment among first-generation and low-income students, citing the same federal funding pressure that had reshaped Columbia's policies days earlier. Trump commuted the sentence of Ozy Media's Carlos Watson and pardoned Nikola founder Trevor Milton, who had donated roughly $2 million to his campaign, eliminating hundreds of millions of dollars in restitution obligations tied to fraud convictions. Dr. Peter Marks, the FDA's top vaccine regulator, resigned after being told to resign or be fired, warning publicly that Health Secretary Kennedy wanted "subservient confirmation" of misinformation rather than scientific accuracy — a resignation that landed in the middle of an active measles outbreak. In Wisconsin, a state Supreme Court race became a flashpoint after Elon Musk spent more than $20 million and offered direct cash payments to voters and petition signers, prompting the state's attorney general to sue to block the payments as illegal vote-buying. Markets fell sharply amid inflation data that exceeded the Federal Reserve's target and new uncertainty over auto tariffs. And two fired Federal Trade Commission commissioners, Rebecca Kelly Slaughter and Alvaro Bedoya, sued over their removal, arguing it violated statutory protections meant to insulate independent agencies from direct presidential control.

Taken as a whole, the week amounted to a test of how many institutional buffers could be pressed at once — the legal profession, the judiciary, the civil service, universities, independent agencies, and the electoral process itself — and how each would respond. Some yielded: Paul Weiss and Skadden settled; Columbia and Michigan reshaped their policies under funding threats. Others resisted and, in at least one case, won outright: Perkins Coie's injunction, and the protective orders shielding Yunseo Chung and Rumeysa Ozturk, showed that courts retained real capacity to intervene when presented with a case. The Signal chat scandal, running from Monday's revelation through Thursday's preservation order, demonstrated both how casually classified military planning could be handled at the highest levels and how difficult it was proving to hold anyone directly accountable for it. None of these threads resolved by Friday. What the week made clear was that the pressure was sustained, coordinated across many fronts simultaneously, and met by a response that was real but far from uniform — a system under strain, still functioning in places, bending in others. ```
